title: Belfast & Donegal
standfirst: Archibald’s Scottish parents and eldest son Thomas of Lifford are probable; Elizabeth is his documented wife. The Killybegs collector is now tentatively placed as Thomas’s son, with his birth unknown. Belfast remains a separate occurrence.
question: Is Archibald of Ramelton’s named eldest son the Thomas documented at Lifford and Raphoe?
answer: Prefer the named eldest son as Thomas of Lifford/Raphoe and the 1614 Glasgow child as the Donegal cleric, both probable. Thomas is now selected as the Killybegs collector James’s uncertain father using the same county and compatible family generations; no record names that father. The inspected tax return supplies a balance under 1728, not a birth or death. Elizabeth is Archibald’s documented wife. 20 October 2026: Killycurragh gains a selected possible Kirknewton connection at 36%, and James-1025’s existing father is reassessed to 32%. The minister’s Irish father is 94% and Margaret’s is 84%; the Scottish identities remain unproved. See the linked Killycurragh generations review.

chapters.title: Dublin: Philip is the preferred father of Thomas, 67%
body: Research rationale: use the combined Dublin family and trade evidence to select a useful working parent, with its unresolved identities explicit.

Select Philip Glasco-146, the provisional elder Dublin watchmaker account, as the probable working father of Thomas Glasco-144 at 67% subjective confidence. The maintained reading of the 1773 advertisement explicitly says that Thomas served his apprenticeship to his father Philip Glasco and subsequently practised in London before returning to his father’s Christ-Church-lane house. Thomas’s 12 December 1773 marriage to Margaret Duffy at neighbouring St Audoen’s supplies a particular same-name adult, same year and immediate locality, rather than a Scotland-wide name comparison. A young tradesman returning to the family business and marrying later that year is the preferred explanation. The later Christ-Church-lane to 20 Ormond Quay sequence supports continuity of the watchmaking business. The separate marriage and apprenticeship evidence together justify preferring Philip to the unsupported Thomas-173 father attachment.

The 67% rates the complete profile-level father proposition, including identification of the 1773 groom with the advertised watchmaker and of the named Philip with the elder account. Neither the marriage index nor the Duffy pedigree gives Thomas’s trade, address or father’s forename. The advertisement is reused from the 7 October full-page OCR reading; its original image was not newly inspected. The older Philip account contains some junior events, so the elder/junior distinction remains material. Thomas’s circa 1753 birth is an estimate: age twenty would make completed apprenticeship plus several years in London compressed, favouring a somewhat older adult without establishing a replacement birth year. No date is changed. The rare surname, close locality and year are correlated clues, not independent parent statements.

Retain Thomas Glasco-173 as an unselected, previously ungraded father alternative, and retain a distinct unrepresented Thomas watchmaker as an identity alternative. Thomas-173, father with Catherine of Sarah in 1760, is chronologically compatible with the trade cluster, but connecting that household to the 1773 groom adds an unsupported generation, whereas the advertisement names Philip. Thomas-143 could represent the tradesman only if his very weak circa 1766 estimate is revised; the date is not a hard exclusion. The 1779 Miss Hynes marriage and the 1785 Mary King licence may concern remarriages, but no spouse death or identity bridge establishes that sequence. No merge, new wife or new child follows.

The current Catherine Mangan mother attachment and Thomas-143 child attachment remain separately ungraded; Philip’s spouse is not thereby proved to be Thomas’s mother. The selected father replaces one existing local working attachment. Two already-catalogued descendants move into the main working component; the old Thomas-173 account remains separate. No new person, live WikiTree edit or confidence-only upgrade is claimed. The earlier Scottish ancestry assigned to Philip remains uncertain and does not become probable through this change.

Check the original 1773 advertisement and marriage entry, the Duffy 1774/1775 probate papers, and Thomas’s London apprenticeship/freedom records for trade, address or named kin. Seek the 1777 Margaret Glasco grant and the full 1777 Philip/Thomas chancery bill before accepting a Duffy–Hynes remarriage or a precise Philip generation.

The 21 October Trinity review adds a probable son, John Glascow/Glasco, to Thomas-144 at 63%, and a probable mother, Eliza Hynes, at 72%. The 1800 entry names father Thomas, a craftsman; the 1784 baptism’s Hynes mother fits the watchmaker’s 1779 Miss Hynes marriage. The student/baptism identity remains probable, with a religious-history gap, and later John profiles remain on HOLD. Philip’s existing 67% father assessment is unchanged.

chapters.title: Killybegs James: a tax balance and a working Donegal father
body: The inspected printed return identifies James Glasgow under Killybegs, opposite the year 1728, with a balance of £34 5s 6d. Its full heading is an account of deceased and dismissed tax collectors’ balances in Ireland as at 5 January 1826, under Land and Assessed Taxes. The entry is therefore retrospective. It is not a customs-collector appointment, an assertion that James lived in 1826, or a recorded birth or death in 1728. The precise meaning of the unlabelled year column is not stated on the inspected pages. Printed p.198 supplies the return heading and p.201 the James entry; Internet Archive leaves 216 and 219 were visually checked on 17 October 2026. The item’s inconsistent catalogue date is not used as the document’s date.

Select Thomas Glasgow-3556 of Lifford/Raphoe as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-3001. Thomas is an established Donegal legal/property actor from the 1684 Raphoe-linked court occurrence through the 1692–1695 Shannon/Ballindrait deeds and the 1701 Exchequer continuation. James belongs to a later dated Donegal account under 1728. The same uncommon surname, regional continuity and compatible succession of legal/property and revenue roles make Thomas a useful preferred existing father account. This extends the recorded Ramelton–Lifford family into the otherwise unattached collector account without inventing an intermediary. It is a regional and generational inference: none of these records names James as Thomas’s son.

The record dates are not measured ages. The 1728 entry may carry an earlier deceased or dismissed officer’s balance, so it cannot select a generation precisely. Archibald Glasgow-1101, Thomas’s probable father, remains a concrete older-family alternative: James might be Thomas’s younger brother or another kinsman rather than his son. An unrelated Donegal or wider Ulster Glasgow family remains possible. The Tyrone James Glasgow-1025 and Belfast Captain James Glasgow-3172 are not merged with this collector or excluded solely by their unproved birth estimates and parent fields. No Scottish-to-Irish migration, exact age, mother, spouse or child of James is inferred. Thomas’s existing probable Archibald father and his other children keep their separate assessments.

Replace the unsupported circa-1650 birth display with Unknown. Use 1728 only as the retrospective account-reference year for research grouping, with birth year unknown. The unlabelled year column does not supply an age or a firm birth boundary; birth could have been substantially earlier. Scotland remains an inherited uncertain birthplace claim; no Irish birthplace is substituted. This correction is independent of the proposed father: the same chronology applies if Thomas is rejected. The old circa-1650 value remains in the imported/current-profile comparison, and all live WikiTree fields are unchanged.

One uncertain local father is newly selected; no confidence upgrade or documentary parentage is claimed. The new link joins the collector’s one-profile component to the existing working family before 1850. Removing the unsupported 1650 chronology changes membership of the current pre-1650/pre-1700 cohorts; that denominator correction is not a family connection. The immutable baseline and separately reported fixed-cohort results are preserved. No mother or identity merge is added.

chapters.title: Glasgow to Donegal: Archibald’s parents, wife and eldest son
body: Prefer the Glasgow child baptised on 19 June 1614 and the Archibaldus Glasgua who graduated M.A. in 1635 as the earlier identity of the Donegal cleric. The uncommon full name, compatible age at graduation, clerical career and 1639 Irish clerk occurrence form a coherent Scottish-to-Irish career. A baptism in 1614 places him at about 21 in 1635 and 25 in 1639. These are conditional ages, not separately recorded ages. No incompatible parentage or simultaneous Scottish household is identified for this proposed cleric. The other known same-generation Scottish Archibald, the Leith man Glasgow-3078, has a separately traced craft career: apprentice to cordiner Thomas Park in October 1639 and shoemaker/heir in May 1647. That positive career sequence makes him a weaker fit to the 1635 graduate and Irish clerk than the 1614 Glasgow child. It is a ranking argument, not an absolute exclusion or an assertion that a man could never change occupation. The Irish testator is securely the Ramelton/Rathmalton cleric by exact name, residence and profession. Assess his existing George Glasgow and Margaret Steuart parent links as probable, reflecting the probable Scottish childhood identification. The baptism explicitly names both parents, so maternity has its own record basis rather than being inferred from George’s spouse field.

No Irish record reviewed names Archibald’s Scottish parents or university. The graduation and 1639 clerk entry do not themselves state the 1614 baptism date. Another Archibald remains possible. This is a preferred combined identity, not documented migration or proof that every early Scottish and Irish occurrence is one man. The quoted baptism witnesses are reused from the maintained reading, not newly checked against an image. Margaret’s own Stewart ancestry, George’s wider family, and the 1647–1661 ministry chronology retain their existing grades.

Betham’s inspected abstract of the April 1673 will of Archibald Glasgow, clerk of Rathmalton, explicitly identifies Thomas Glasgow as his eldest son. Prefer the existing Thomas of Lifford/Raphoe account for that son: the exact uncommon name, the adjacent Donegal setting and the next adult generation fit the independently documented Raphoe-linked court case of 1684, Lifford occurrence of 1689 and Ballindrait/Shannon deeds of 1692–1695. The 1692 Creighton court association and later estate material strengthen the continuity of that adult Thomas account; they are not independent statements of his parentage. The full local and generational fit warrants a probable father link to Archibald. A further unique estate or household identifier would strengthen it, but its absence does not require leaving this coherent family at merely uncertain.

Betham gives the son no age, residence, spouse or estate. He could be another Thomas, so the Lifford identification remains inferred rather than documented. The profile’s before-1671/circa-1670 birth estimates are not ages supplied by the abstract or court records and are not used as proof of either identity or exclusion. No maternity is assigned to Thomas from Elizabeth’s status as Archibald’s wife. Nathaniel and George remain Thomas’s separately assessed children; the later Killybegs James and Belfast Captain James are not made relatives by this review.

Betham’s inspected pre-destruction abstract explicitly identifies Elizabeth as wife of Archibald Glasgow, clerk of Rathmalton. The existing Elizabeth account represents that record-defined wife, while Archibald’s Irish identity is secured by exact name, clerical designation and residence. The spouse relationship is documented independently of the probable Scottish baptism and Thomas-to-Lifford identifications. The provisionally read M’Auley surname is retained as a reading, not installed as a certain surname.

The abstract is not the complete will; April 1673 is the will date and 1677 the separate probate index date. It does not establish a wedding date, Elizabeth’s birth or parents, or her maternity of every named child. Her existing profile name and estimates are preserved.

Four existing assessments change: two probable Scottish parent links for Archibald, a probable Archibald–Thomas father link, and a documented Archibald–Elizabeth marriage. This is a confidence review of existing attachments, not four new relatives. No live WikiTree save, identity merge, new mother for Thomas or new manuscript inspection is claimed. The Irish male line has four pre-1850 profile accounts including its current descendants; those descendants’ own uncertain links are not upgraded wholesale.

chapters.title: Probable traditional ancestry; the Leitrim identity remains open
body: The explicit family-history roles William Glasgow-591 → John Glasgow-551 → Hugh Glasgow-548 are now assessed as probable locally. The pedigree names the fathers, and its nearer household can be correlated with the Pennsylvania family. This is an inference from one retrospective account, not a contemporary Irish parent record.

This does not strengthen John Glasgow-3960’s very uncertain placement as John-551’s son. Identity between those two Johns remains a live alternative, and no Tyrone–Leitrim migration, new wife, mother or Scottish record identity is inferred. The complete ancestry review is in the Tamlaght study.

The Killycurragh review of 20 October 2026 separates two successive Williams and selects the Coleraine minister John’s father at 94% and his wife Margaret’s father, William Glasgow-2426, at 84%. James Glasgow-1025’s existing father Glasgow-1026 is reassessed from 12% to 32%; the older Killycurragh William is tentatively identified with William Glasgow-1318, giving the younger Cunningham husband a possible father at 36%. These are a distinct Kirknewton–Tyrone comparison and do not strengthen the separate Leitrim identification.

chapters.title: Leitrim and Tyrone: a very uncertain John-to-John connection
body: Glasgow-551, the John said in the later family history to have found a home in County Tyrone, is selected as a very uncertain working father of Glasgow-3960, gentleman of Gortigillagh, County Leitrim, recorded in 1728. This develops the comparison already recorded in both case files. Keeping their current estimated generations separate gives about 1681 for the older John and about 1705 for the witness: a possible 24-year father–son interval. The proposed connection gives the Leitrim household a testable place alongside the early Irish family tradition. Its preference over an identity match depends on retaining those two estimated generations; neither birth year is independent evidence for paternity. The same uncommon surname and an early Irish setting support investigating kinship, but do not determine its degree. There is no named-father clause or documented Tyrone–Leitrim migration, and no place of birth is inferred from this link.

The first dated occurrence used here is 30 May 1728, registered 11 July: Registry of Deeds memorial 38213, volume 57, page 235. The existing derivative abstract names John Glasgow, gentleman of Gortigillagh, County Leitrim, witnessing a transaction between James Johnston of Cashellmenon, County Donegal, and Robert Johnston of Aghadunvane, County Leitrim, with Bartley McGowan and John Gilhuly. No original has been newly inspected. “1707” is an older inferred birth boundary from assuming an adult witness aged at least 21; it is not a 1707 record. The structured about-1705 birth and County Leitrim birthplace remain estimates, not documentary dates or proof of origin. The notes favour Gortaggle in Annaduff, supported by the near-contemporary Gortogill/Cortogill forms; the older biography favours Gortnasillagh in Rossinver. Both locality assessments remain visible. This parent model uses County Leitrim only and does not resolve the townland to manufacture geographic proximity.

Identity between the two Johns is a live alternative, already raised by the earlier review: the witness could have been much older than his present estimate. If that identity is established, this provisional father edge must be withdrawn as a duplicate-person construction, rather than retained as two generations. A brother, uncle, more distant relative, or another Glasgow family is also possible. The older John’s own descent from Glasgow-591 comes from late family tradition and receives no new support here. His roughly 1681 birth was calculated from his son Hugh’s estimated generation; the broader 1656–1688 range in the profile is not a measured age. No wife or mother is supplied for either John.

Glasgow-3124 of Aghadonvane already has Glasgow-3960 attached as father, without a certainty mark. That existing link remains unproved and is not a new connection or a confidence upgrade. John’s 1728 Johnston/McGowan associations can be compared with James’s 1779 lease and marriage-articles witnesses: a repeated local social network supports investigating continuity, not the exact father–son relationship. The 15 August 1779 lease, registered 10 August 1780, names James as esquire of Aghadonvane and uses Robert and William, young sons of James Johnston of Kinlough, as measuring lives. Those lives are not called Glasgow relatives. The 2 October 1779 marriage articles name James Glasgow, Edmund/Edmond Connolly and Andrew McGowan as witnesses. James’s present circa-1750 birth would make the circa-1705 John about 45 at his birth; both dates are estimates. An older James or a different generation remains possible. No intervening ancestor is invented.

The previously queued Findmypast notes give more detail for James’s 1782 probate occurrence: Betham’s Prerogative intestate-administration abstract is indexed on 24 January 1782, with Catherine as spouse (IRE/NAI/GENABS/00401119/1 and /2). This narrows the earlier will-versus-administration question at transcript level. The abstract image still needs checking before identifying Catherine as administratrix/widow or assigning an exact death boundary. It supplies no evidence that John was James’s father, that Catherine was his mother, or that the Tyrone John was his grandfather. The published Montgomery pedigree identifies Glasgow-3958 as James’s daughter; it does not extend the Glasgow ancestry.

One very uncertain father is newly selected, conditional on treating the two John accounts as different generations. This is a working hypothesis, not a proved Tyrone–Leitrim family or an independently supported migration. The identity alternative, guessed dates, townland disagreement and unproved existing John–James link remain explicit. No merge, new mother, changed vital field, certainty upgrade or live WikiTree save is claimed. Connectivity counts retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates.

chapters.title: Dublin watchmakers and Irvine: two uncertain fathers
body: Select Thomas Glasgow-1242 as the uncertain working father of Philip Glasco-146. The preferred model uses Glasco-146 as the elder Dublin watchmaker account, retaining the 1711 Scottish child Glasgow-1241 as a separate possible account of the same man. That child’s Uphall index names father Thomas; his existing research already retains the elder watchmaker as a compatible adult identity. The Glasco-146 account has the Christ Church Lane watchmaking association in 1752, an estimated birth about 1715 and a younger Philip in its tree family, which suit that provisional elder role. The four-year difference from the 1711 baptism is between a record and an unsupported estimate, not a concrete identity conflict. This materialises the existing Scottish candidate at low confidence; it does not prove migration or two distinct elder Philips.

The Dublin records name no Scottish parents, birthplace or apprenticeship, so the Scottish child and elder watchmaker may be different men. The fresh Glasco-146 biography itself mixes the 1752 watchmaker with junior notices of 1765,1768 and 1770. Its c.1715 birth and the c.1740 birth of Glasco-147 are tree estimates, not evidence selecting a generation. If Glasco-146 instead represents the junior, the elder Philip is an alternative father-generation placement and the Thomas link would need revision; no competing father is attached alongside it. The elder placement is a preferred working interpretation of the profile’s trade/address and family structure, not a claim that every event in that biography belongs to him. The junior’s 1765 unnamed-wife death,1768 Teresa Plunkett marriage and reported 1770 death remain with the younger documentary account Glasgow-3932. Glasco-147 is a strongly supported duplicate account of that younger man, but its quoted 1772 younger/inventory wording was not independently rechecked here and establishes neither the estimated birth nor a newly verified father clause; a grant date is not a death date. No merge, spouse transfer or new child attachment follows. Catherine Mangan is called Glasco-146’s mother in its prose but spouse in its structured family; the 1750 report describes the elder’s bride only as the widow Mangan, and the 1760 report gives no forename. Neither record proves maternity. Preserve the existing Mangan/Braccan and younger-parent fields as qualified leads; do not add a mother for Glasco-146. The father Thomas is common to the retained 1711 child records, while the 3 June Uphall versus 21 October Linlithgow Philip entries and their maternal readings remain unreconciled; Jean Duncan is not transferred as Glasco-146’s mother. The 1777 probate/court occurrence does not establish survival after 1772. The local elder account uses 1772 as an uncertain death year through the selected identity, retaining the old after 1772 value and all junior events in the comparison.

Select Hugh Glasgow-3109, father with Jean Service at Irvine in 1696, as the very low-confidence working father of James Glasgow-4158, father with Margaret/Marion Rae at Irvine in 1721–1723. This extends an actual local household across a compatible generation. A James born in the later 1690s could be a son of the 1696 household and an adult father by 1721; this is a compatibility example, not a new birth estimate. Hugh’s proposed identity with the 1676 Kilwinning child would make him a young father in the 1690s, which fits that example. The shared uncommon surname, same parish and two successive family generations favour this existing named parent model; no register entry names James’s father.

James could instead be a son of the Irvine John-2475/Isabell Kyle family, Michael-1406’s household, another Ayrshire family, or an unrecorded father. The named James child of John/Isabell indexed in 1711 would be only about ten at the 1721 fatherhood if baptised as an infant, so he is a weaker identity candidate unless an older-baptism explanation is established. James’s before 1702 boundary is an adult-status estimate, not an actual birth. If James were substantially older, Hugh’s proposed 1676 child identity would become less plausible; no date is changed to make either hypothesis fit. The older Hugh/Hew account, its existing uncertain parents, Jean Service/Mary Dean identity sequence and earlier alternatives remain as previously assessed. James’s merged Margaret/Marion Rae household remains a working combined father account; no remarriage or equivalence between the mothers is proved. The 1740 Prosperity of Irvine shipmaster is still a possible occupational identity only, with no transfer of occupation, voyage or trade to this father. Jean Service is not selected as James’s mother solely from Hugh’s co-parentage.

Two newly selected uncertain fathers, no new mother, identity merge, certainty upgrade or live WikiTree save. Existing newspaper/parish reviews supply the historical comparisons; three Open/non-living WikiTree profiles were read anonymously to reconcile their current wording. The elder’s 1772 death is conditional on the selected adult identity; no birth is changed. Possible duplicate profile accounts and inherited uncertain routes remain explicit limitations of the working connectivity score.

The anonymous Open-profile capture of Glasgow-3932 on 16 October 2026 contains Robert Glasgow’s Kilrea 1827 biography, not the Dublin watchmaker. The entire misplaced text is also preserved in the captured biography of the correct Robert Glasgow-3897. A complete sourced Dublin replacement is prepared locally; the real current biography remains available in the comparison, with its hash retained. No Robert birth, relatives or life events are transferred to Philip. The structured Dublin profile and the current Glasco-147/Teresa Plunkett family support retaining the earlier strong same-person match between the two younger-Philip profiles, without a live merge or duplicate spouse attachment.

chapters.title: Glenarm and Stevenston: two selected uncertain fathers
body: Select Robert Glaskow of Larne, Glasgow-3970, as the very low-confidence working father of Elizabeth Glasgow-3961, the Eliz Glascho at Glenarm Town in 1669. Robert is an older recorded adult at Larne in 1653, and the existing uncertain paternal family already includes John Glasgow-3913 and James Glasgow-1081, the adjacent Jo/James Glascho householders at Kilwaughter in the same 1669 roll. Elizabeth shares their unusual recorded Glascho form and the east-Antrim setting. Her assumed adult-householder generation in 1669 can be a daughter generation of the earlier Larne man. This extends an existing local family explanation rather than inventing an unnamed father; no record calls Elizabeth his daughter or John’s sister.

Glenarm Town and Kilwaughter Demesne are distinct places in neighbouring lower and upper Glenarm baronies, not one household or consecutive entries. Elizabeth’s forename, surname form and regional date pattern support a family comparison but do not distinguish daughter from sister, niece, cousin or unrelated namesake. The tax entry does not state whether Glasgow was her birth or married surname, whether she was a widow, or her age. A wife/widow identity within another Glasgow household therefore remains possible. Her circa-1650 birth and the competing before-about-1648 adult estimate are inferences, not ages that establish a generation. The Larne man’s possible identity with the 1618 Scottish child remains uncertain, as do his existing Kilwaughter sons and his own selected Scottish parents. No mother is selected for Elizabeth; neither the elder Jonet Cunningham nor the younger Janet Cunningham is transferred to her as mother. Existing chronology, the possible James identities and the hearsay status of the Larne allegations remain unchanged.

Select John Glasgow-3375, the father associated with Barbara Alason/Allason at Kilwinning in 1679 and 1689, as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-4170, father with Mary Auld at Stevenston in 1717–1718. This is a low/very low-confidence regional household placement. The recorded couple supplies a compatible parent generation, and their son John Glasgow-1434, indexed at Kilwinning in 1679, is already a possible identity for the John who had children with Margaret Cowan at Stevenston in 1701 and 1706. That existing route gives a specific neighbouring-parish family comparison for James’s later Stevenston household. The preferred provisional model places James alongside that John as a possible paternal brother. It does not identify a baptism for James or claim that the 1717–1718 entries name his parents.

James’s before-1698 birth is an existing estimated adult boundary from his 1717 fatherhood, not a baptism or an age. His actual birth could fit a child of the Kilwinning couple, but the route also depends on the unproved identification of their 1679 son with the Stevenston adult. The John-3375 and Rev. John-1073 profiles remain possible accounts of one man; no merge, duplicate resolution, ministry or new son of the minister is established here. The shared John-1604 parent and older family scaffold remain uncertain. The already selected uncertain son James-3105, father at Kilwinning in 1689 with Margaret Park, is a serious surviving identity alternative for James-4170: an earlier Park household followed by a later Auld household is possible, but no occupation, age or marriage bridge identifies them. Retain both accounts without counting the father selection as proof of two distinct James sons. Other local fathers, including the older Matthew of Pyperheugh as a possible father or earlier kinsman, remain alternatives; his 1665 spouse entry alone supplies no James child, and the long interval to 1717 requires caution. No mother is selected for James: Barbara’s known maternity of the 1679 child does not establish James’s mother, and no marriage to Mary Auld is invented beyond the recorded parent pair.

Two newly selected uncertain fathers using existing records and household comparisons; no new mother, original-source inspection, certainty upgrade, identity merge or live WikiTree save. Existing vital dates, age assumptions, source readings and earlier pending amendments remain intact. The two suggested paternal-sibling relationships depend on the selected fathers and the older uncertain identity/parent links; they are not independent sibling attestations. Connectivity counts retained profile accounts, so possible duplicates remain a limitation of the working score.

chapters.period: 1618–1665 · two uncertain fathers and one uncertain mother
chapters.title: Stevenston and South Leith: selected uncertain families
body: Select John Glasgow-1030 as the very low-confidence working father of Matthew Glasgow-3538 of Pyperheugh, Stevenston. John and Jonet Mathie married in Glasgow on 25 January 1618 and have recorded children in the following decade. A son of that household, born in the 1620s, could be an adult spouse in the 1665 testament index that names Matthew. This is a compatible generation, not a new birth estimate. The existing Mathie–Glasgow network supplies a positive social route between Glasgow and Stevenston: David Mathy and Robert Glasgow were co-witnesses in 1554, while Matthew Glasgow and John Mathie were together at Ardeer Nether in 1559–60. The later marriage joins those surname networks. The recurrence of Matthew in the same parish makes this existing household a useful selected descent hypothesis; it does not identify a father in a record.

No inspected record names Matthew’s parents or connects his Pyperheugh household directly to the Glasgow couple. The route depends on Jonet’s unproved place in the older Mathie network and on the probable identification of the 1618 husband with Ninian’s brother John represented by Glasgow-1030. John’s confident Robert Glasgow-1096 father assessment remains conditional on that adult identification and is not newly upgraded. Other Stevenston fathers, collateral descent from the 1559–60 Matthew, and an unrelated same-name family remain possible. The 106-year interval rules out identity with that earlier adult; no missing generation is invented and no direct father edge to him is selected. The Saltcoats sailor John, spouse of Isobell Gray, remains a separate record-defined household; this model does not merge them. The 1619 baptismal witness Mathew Will is not Matthew Mathie or proof of a Glasgow relative.

Assess Jonet Mathie-159 separately as Matthew’s uncertain working mother. Her recorded 1618 marriage and maternity in the following decade provide an actual couple and a compatible childbearing generation; her circa-1597 birth is an estimate. The Mathie associations in Stevenston are the proposed route for this household’s connection to Pyperheugh. Selecting her is a conditional couple hypothesis, not an automatic consequence of attaching John. It has very low confidence: no record calls Matthew her son, no Mathie ancestor is newly attached, and another mother remains possible. The paternal and maternal selections share the same network argument and are correlated, not two independent confirmations.

Select William Glasgow-3075, the Leith mealmaker, as the low-confidence working father of Margaret Glasgow-3186, indexed marrying George Lyell at South Leith on 28 November 1633. William’s household is documented at Leith, with a proposed 10 July 1610 local marriage and a son Archibald baptised in 1618, securely linked to the adult mealmaker by the 1639 apprenticeship and 1647 service of heir. A daughter marrying in 1633 fits that established household generation. Shared surname, the same parish and a coherent marriage/child generation favour this named household over a newly invented father. No source calls Margaret his daughter. Her circa-1610 birth remains an inherited estimate and supplies no independent evidence of William’s paternity.

Retain the strongest specific alternative: Betham’s pedigree of Archibald Glasgow, Rathmalton clerk, whose will was dated April 1673, names Margaret as his only daughter, wife of an unnamed Cairns and mother of Thomas Cairns. The documentary father–daughter relationship is explicit, but identifying that Margaret with Glasgow-3186 remains unproved. A first Lyell marriage in 1633 permits a later Cairns marriage. The preferred William placement avoids requiring that unproved Scottish–Irish identity and remarriage. It also avoids tension with the probable identification of Archibald Glasgow-1101 as the child baptised in Glasgow in 1614 and the 1635 graduate: that child would be an implausible father of a 1633 bride. This is a ranking consideration, not an exclusion: the Scottish identity is unproved, and a baptism is not necessarily an infant’s birth. The new uncertain William field must not be used as a concrete father conflict to reject the Rathmalton candidate. A different South Leith Glasgow father also remains possible. No mother is selected: Catherine Fraith/Fraser’s 1610 bride identity and Christian Scot’s separate Glasgow household remain qualified. William’s testament names Archibald as lawful son and sole executor, not only child; omission of Margaret neither excludes her nor proves kinship.

Margaret’s copied source string records the 28 November 1633 South Leith marriage, OPR 692/2, 90/264, FR3038. Its truncated surname string ASGOWE is retained in the profile comparison, not silently expanded as an original-image reading. The old exact-looking birth year is displayed as circa 1610, an inherited estimate with no age record. South Leith is the marriage place, not an evidenced death place; death date and place remain unknown. Matthew’s before-1650 birth remains uncertain, and his inherited Stevenson birthplace is not proved by the Stevenston residence. The 24 April 1665 date belongs to Jonet Cowan’s testament-index entry, not Matthew’s birth, marriage or death. No original source was newly inspected.

Two newly selected uncertain fathers and one separately assessed uncertain mother; no live WikiTree save, identity merge, new original inspection or certainty upgrade. Matthew’s two proposed parents form a correlated household hypothesis; Margaret’s Rathmalton identity alternative remains open. chapters.title: A Belfast shipmaster
body: PRONI maritime material identifies Captain James Glasgow or Glascow as a Belfast-associated shipmaster active by 1667. In 1669/70, James Glasco, mariner, was admitted and sworn a free commoner of Belfast.
A 1686 Belfast will extract is a lead for further reading, not a proved death date; no inspected source names James's parents, spouse or children.

chapters.title: An Irish father and his named son
body: The newly inspected Betham manuscript names Archibald Glasgow of Rathmalton, County Donegal, clerk; Elizabeth (surname provisionally M’Auley); Thomas Glasgow, eldest son; and Margaret, only daughter. The exact clerical designation and residence identify the Irish testator confidently.
April 1673 is the will date, not death or probate. The separate will index gives probate in 1677. Betham’s manuscript is a genealogical abstract derived from the will, not the complete original.

The named son is now the probable identity of Thomas of Lifford/Raphoe; a distinctive relative, associate or estate connection is the next test for a higher grade. Archibald’s Scottish childhood identification is also probable. Thomas’s proposed fatherhood of Nathaniel remains a separate unresolved question.

chapters.title: Thomas in the Raphoe legal network
body: Thomas Glasgow appears in a Raphoe-linked court case in 1684, at Lifford in the 1689 attainder list, and in Ballindrait and Shannon property transactions from 1692 to 1695.
A 1701 Exchequer entry is a high-confidence continuation. These records show a documented adult actor, not his birth, family or beneficial ownership of every property named.

chapters.title: A Killybegs account occurrence
body: The inspected printed return identifies James Glasgow under Killybegs, opposite the year 1728, with a balance of £34 5s 6d. Its full heading is an account of deceased and dismissed tax collectors’ balances in Ireland as at 5 January 1826, under Land and Assessed Taxes. The entry is therefore retrospective. It is not a customs-collector appointment, an assertion that James lived in 1826, or a recorded birth or death in 1728. The precise meaning of the unlabelled year column is not stated on the inspected pages. Printed p.198 supplies the return heading and p.201 the James entry; Internet Archive leaves 216 and 219 were visually checked on 17 October 2026. The item’s inconsistent catalogue date is not used as the document’s date.

Replace the unsupported circa-1650 birth display with Unknown. Use 1728 only as the retrospective account-reference year for research grouping, with birth year unknown. The unlabelled year column does not supply an age or a firm birth boundary; birth could have been substantially earlier. Scotland remains an inherited uncertain birthplace claim; no Irish birthplace is substituted. This correction is independent of the proposed father: the same chronology applies if Thomas is rejected. The old circa-1650 value remains in the imported/current-profile comparison, and all live WikiTree fields are unchanged.
Thomas of Lifford is selected as an uncertain local father. Archibald, other Glasgow families and other degrees of kinship remain alternatives; Belfast Captain James is not merged with the collector.

chapters.title: A named household and separate regional occurrences
body: Archibald’s fatherhood of a named son Thomas is explicit; identifying him as Thomas of Lifford is probable. James of Killybegs is now a selected uncertain son of that Thomas, without documentary kinship.
Belfast Captain James remains a separate account. No connection to Kilwaughter or a named Irish founder is proved by the collector’s balance.

chapters.title: Crossle’s Archbold Glascow clerk entry (15 October 2026)
body: Crossle’s abstract names Archbold Glascow, clerk, on 9 December 1639. The two dated transcript IDs point to the same image and document 849; the undated Smith VII entry is document 501 on a different image and is not a proved duplicate. The originals remain unread, so Archibald Glasgow-1101 is a plausible candidate only.

The earlier 1647–1661 minister leads were misfiled under Thomas Glasgow-3556 and are now recorded with Archibald Glasgow-1101. A separate 1657 catalogue lead remains unresolved. No Thomas-son identity or relationship-certainty upgrade is made.
